title: FRM Current Issues, Lesson 5: Climate risk and climate stress testing
subtitle: Physical risk, transition risk, and a problem with no historical data to calibrate against
whyItMatters: Supervisors in many countries have brought climate stress testing into their banking oversight programmes. It is also the first risk problem where the whole toolkit built on historical data is close to useless.
openingQuestion: How does physical risk differ from transition risk within climate risk?
openingOptions: Physical risk is natural disaster, transition risk is policy
Physical risk applies to tangible assets while transition risk applies to financial assets
Physical risk plays out in the short term while transition risk only appears fifty years from now
Physical risk is borne by companies while transition risk is borne by the government budget
explanation: Climate risk splits into two branches with entirely different mechanisms. Physical risk is storms, floods and drought destroying assets and interrupting operations. Transition risk is the damage from the move to a low-carbon economy itself: carbon taxes, new regulation, substitute technologies that strand existing assets early. For a carbon-intensive business the second branch is usually the larger one - and it can appear suddenly even though the transition itself is slow.

diagram.label: Physical risk: acute disasters and chronic change
Transition risk: policy, technology and market preferences shift
Both feed into credit, market and operational risk
No matching historical data, so long-horizon scenarios have to be used

realWorldExample.company: Why a climate stress test is unlike every other stress test
realWorldExample.description: A conventional stress test takes a shock from the past as its template - the 2008 crisis, a sudden rate rise - and asks whether today's balance sheet could withstand it. A climate stress test has no template to take: no period in modern financial history resembles what is being modelled, and the horizon is decades rather than a few quarters. So it is a scenario exercise rather than a statistical one.

quiz.question: What is a stranded asset in the context of transition risk?
options: An asset that loses its value early because policy or technology has changed
An asset that cannot be sold because the secondary market is illiquid
An asset frozen by a supervisor during an investigation into a breach of the rules
An asset located in a geographic area with a high future risk of natural disaster
quiz.explanation: A coal mine or a thermal power plant can retain its full technical value while losing its economic value once regulation tightens or a substitute technology gets cheaper. For a bank, that is collateral evaporating while the loan stays exactly where it was. Temporary illiquidity is a market condition that reverses, a regulatory freeze is a legal event unrelated to climate, and location in a disaster-prone area is physical risk rather than transition risk - the very distinction this lesson turns on.

quiz.question: Why is the long time horizon such a distinctive difficulty in climate risk?
options: Because financial models cannot compute anything beyond a five-year period
Because it runs far past the planning cycle and the tenure of the decision-maker
Because climate data is only published by meteorological agencies every ten years
Because a discount rate cannot be determined for maturities that long
quiz.explanation: This is known as the tragedy of the horizon: the largest damage falls outside the period for which today's decision-makers are answerable, so the incentive to act early is weak even though acting late costs far more. Financial models handle multi-decade horizons routinely - a thirty-year mortgage is priced that way - and long-dated discount rates, while contested, are estimated all the time. Climate data is published continuously rather than once a decade.

quiz.question: How does a climate stress test differ from a traditional stress test?
options: It produces a binding capital requirement rather than an indicative figure
It applies only to banks with lending exposure to the energy sector
It is a long-horizon scenario exercise that cannot be calibrated from past data
It is performed daily rather than on the annual cycle used elsewhere
quiz.explanation: There is no precedent in modern financial history to calibrate against, so the result depends almost entirely on the scenario assumptions. Its value lies in forcing the institution to see where the portfolio is exposed, rather than in the final number. Most climate exercises so far have been explicitly non-binding for capital, they cover every sector because climate feeds into agriculture, property and manufacturing alike, and they run on multi-year cycles because building the scenarios takes months.

quiz.question: A factory in a flood plain and a coal-fired plant facing a carbon tax - which risk type is each?
options: The first is transition risk and the second is physical risk
Both are physical risk, since both originate in the climate
The first is physical risk and the second is transition risk
Both are transition risk, since policy is what causes each of them
quiz.explanation: Physical risk is damage caused by the weather event itself - flood, storm, drought. Transition risk comes from the human response to climate: taxes, regulation, substitute technology, changing preferences. Separating the two is the first step because they strike different assets on different timetables, and a portfolio can be heavily exposed to one while barely touched by the other.

quiz.question: Why can transition risk appear abruptly even though the transition itself is slow?
options: Because markets reprice in one move when expectations turn, not gradually year by year
Because climate regulation always takes effect the moment it is announced
Because substitute technologies usually emerge with no advance warning at all
Because the physical effects of climate change are arriving faster than every scientific forecast
quiz.explanation: Asset prices reflect expectations, and expectations move in steps: a policy decision, a technology cost threshold being crossed. The physical process is slow, but the market's acknowledgement of it happens over a handful of sessions. Regulation almost always has a long implementation period, and substitute technologies come down a visible cost curve for years before they matter - what is abrupt is not the underlying change but the moment prices admit it.

practicePrompt.question: A coal-fired power plant has 18 years of technical life left, but a new rule just enacted forces it to stop operating after 7. The bank has lent against it on a 12-year term. What should it do?
options: Recognise a stranded asset and review the term of the loan
Change nothing, since the plant still works perfectly well technically
Wait until the rule actually takes effect before reassessing anything
Reclassify the loan under physical risk rather than transition risk
practicePrompt.explanation: A stranded asset is one that keeps its full TECHNICAL value while losing its ECONOMIC value early, and this is the cleanest example there is: the plant can run for 18 years, but the cash flow only runs for 7. The 12-year loan therefore loses its source of repayment from year eight, and the collateral has close to no liquidation value precisely when it is needed. Waiting for the rule to take effect is five years too late: the economic value falls on the day the rule is ENACTED, not the day it bites - which is also why transition risk appears abruptly even though the transition is slow.

keyTakeaways: Physical risk is damage from natural disaster; transition risk comes from policy and technology
A stranded asset keeps its technical value but loses its economic value early
The tragedy of the horizon: the largest damage falls outside the tenure of today's decision-makers
A climate stress test is a scenario exercise and cannot be calibrated from history

summary.keyIdea: Climate is the first risk that forces the industry to manage something seriously without any corresponding historical data
summary.commonMistake: Reading the output of a climate stress test as a measured figure, when it mostly reflects the scenario assumptions that were chosen
summary.action: Read a climate stress test by looking at where the portfolio is exposed, rather than stopping at the loss number

application.title: Look at a portfolio through the transition lens
application.message: For any portfolio, try asking: if a meaningful carbon tax arrived tomorrow, which of these assets would lose value first?
application.secondary: That question tends to reveal sector concentration that a standard allocation table does not show.

sections.text: Every tool in the FRM programme relies on historical data to some degree. Climate risk is the first problem where that approach does not work.

left.label: Physical risk
left.text: Acute: storms, floods and wildfires destroying collateral. Chronic: rising sea levels and shifting rainfall reducing the productivity of a whole region.

right.label: Transition risk
right.text: Carbon taxes, new regulation, substitute technology and changing preferences strand assets early - even ones that still work perfectly well technically.

sections.text: Climate is not a separate risk type standing beside credit and market risk - it is a source that causes those. A flood destroying a borrower's factory is credit risk; a carbon tax knocking down a sector's share price is market risk; a flooded head office is operational risk.

sections.label: The tragedy of the horizon
sections.text: Most of the damage falls beyond the tenure of the executive team, beyond the planning cycle, and beyond the maturity of many of the loans. The incentive to act today is therefore weak, even though acting late costs far more - which is why this area has had to be driven by supervisors.
Climate is not a new risk type, it is a new source of the existing ones

sections.title: Two channels, and where they land in the books
sections.subtitle: There is no line called climate risk - it appears as credit, market and operational risk

concepts.def: Storms, floods, drought and rising seas damage collateral and interrupt the borrower's cash flow. It enters credit risk through both PD and LGD, and operational risk through the bank's own premises.

Carbon prices, new regulation, technological change and shifting consumer preferences erode the value of the borrower's business model. It enters credit risk in high-emitting sectors and market risk through the repricing of assets.

Strong, early policy action means high transition risk but low physical risk; inaction means the reverse. So the worst scenario for a bank portfolio is not the worst scenario for the climate, and that is where scenarios are most often built wrongly.

sections.label: The tragedy of the horizon
sections.text: Most of the damage falls beyond the tenure of the executive team, beyond the business planning cycle, and beyond the maturity of most loans. A 25-year mortgage carries sea-level risk; a bank planning three years ahead cannot see it. And because there is no historical data to calibrate against - no time series exists for a fivefold rise in the carbon price - scenario analysis replaces the statistical model, and at that point the assumptions become the most important part of the result. What has to be disclosed is not the final number but the set of assumptions that produced it.

lines: With no data to calibrate against, scenarios replace models and the assumptions become the most important part.
Next lesson: another transition that has already been completed, and the lessons it left behind.
